problem: Consider the curve ${e}^{x}-{e}^{y}=y.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-3$ on the curve at the point where $y=0,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.

feedback.problem: Consider the curve $-{y}^{3}+2(x-2)^{2}=10.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{4}$ on the curve at the point where $x=3,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
feedback.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-{y}^{3}+2(x-2)^{2} & =10 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{y}^{3}+2(x-2)^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{y}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2(x-2)^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(-{y}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2(x-2)^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (-3{y}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4(x-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{4}$ and $x=3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (-3{y}^{2})+\frac{1}{4}\cdot 4(3-2) & =0 \\ (-3{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=3$ into the equation of the curve. 

At the point where $x=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-{y}^{3}+2(3-2)^{2} & =10 \\ -{y}^{3}+2 & =10 \\ {y}^{3} & =-8 \\ y & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $y=-2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-3(-2)^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+1 & =0 \\ -12\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+1 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$
